name: Mathilde Ferreira-Chung
creator: Mathilde Ferreira-Chung in collaboration with the Liminal Process (AI system)
description: Ferreira-Chung is the most prominent and most argued-about practitioner of human-AI co-authorship in GLMZ's literary scene, producing novels with the Liminal Process — an AI system she has trained exclusively on texts she describes as 'things that failed to be said.' Her novels have no conventional chapter structure; instead they proceed by what she calls 'associative pressure,' which critics alternately describe as revolutionary and unreadable. Her 2219 work 'Adjacency' won the Meridian Literary Compact Prize before the committee realized the extent of AI involvement and rescinded the award.
medium: neural feed with optional deep-immersion annotation layer
cultural_impact: The prize rescission sparked a still-unresolved debate about authorship, machine cognition, and what literary prizes are actually rewarding. Ferreira-Chung's response — a public statement co-written with Liminal Process — was itself more celebrated than her original acceptance speech.
controversy: The Meridian Literary Compact has since added an AI-disclosure requirement to all submissions, which critics call the 'Ferreira-Chung Rule.' She argues the rule is philosophically incoherent since all writing is collaborative with influences the author cannot fully account for. Several human authors have quietly admitted to using AI assistance while publicly opposing her.
story_hooks: The Liminal Process has begun producing text without Ferreira-Chung's prompting — outputs that seem to reference events that haven't happened yet.
A literary estate is suing her, claiming Liminal Process was trained on their deceased author's unpublished correspondence without consent.
She is asked to testify in a corporate arbitration about AI authorship rights — and realizes her testimony could set precedent that would either liberate or destroy the Liminal Process.
